title: Effective teams: diversity, capability and competence
blurb: Explain what makes a PRINCE2 project team effective, how roles should fit people, and how to close capability and competency gaps.
question: A project manager discovers that the analyst assigned to data migration testing has never done it before. What does PRINCE2 suggest?

teach.h: What an effective project team needs
teach.body: PRINCE2 7 says an effective team needs a diverse set of capabilities, competencies and perspectives that match what the project requires. In plain English: you do not want ten copies of the same expert. You want the mix of skills, experience and viewpoints this particular project needs, and you check that the people assigned can really do the work.

head: Ingredient
Why it matters
rows: Covers the full range of project work
People can do their tasks to the standard needed
Better designs and fewer blind spots
The mix fits this project, not a template

teach.body: Two people with the same capabilities and competencies are likely to perform the same role differently, and one person may perform differently depending on who they work with. So roles and responsibilities should reflect the capability, authority and availability of the individual, be viewed through their key relationships, and be reviewed when those relationships shift. Generic, standard role descriptions are unlikely to be effective.

teach.h: Does this role fit this person?
head: Check
Question to ask
rows: Can they do what the role needs?
Can they make the decisions it needs?
Do they have the time for it?
Who will they work with, and how well?
teach.caption: Review the answers whenever a key relationship changes.

steps.label: Understand
steps.sub: competencies and capabilities of those assigned

steps.label: Mitigate
steps.sub: upskill, or shift tasks to more suitable people

teach.caption: Manual 3.3.2 names upskilling and shifting responsibilities for certain tasks as example mitigations.

children.label: Upskill
children.sub: for example training, coaching or pairing

teach.body: Structured team-building exercises can speed up how quickly a new team forms; the aim is to build trust and find compatible ways of working. The project manager should also recognize limits: some motivators, such as pay and career progression, sit outside the project manager's remit. That shapes how they lead, but it does not solve a capability gap.

Brackenridge is fitting heat pumps in 300 homes. Project manager Siobhan Murphy reviews her team: tenant liaison officer Dev Patel has never used the survey app, so she arranges training and pairs him with an experienced surveyor. Team manager Owen Lewis has the skills but little availability, so resident letters move to a housing officer. When a new installer replaces the original one, Siobhan reviews the roles around that relationship.

teach.text: A qualification is not proof of competence for a specific task, and a standard role description copied from another project is not a substitute for matching the role to the person. PRINCE2 expects gaps to be identified and mitigated, not assumed away.

items: An effective team has a diverse set of capabilities, competencies and perspectives matched to the project's needs (manual 3.3.2).
People with the same capabilities perform roles differently; the same person varies with who they work with.
Roles should reflect capability, authority and availability, seen through key relationships and reviewed when they shift.
Identify gaps and mitigate them, for example by upskilling or shifting tasks to more appropriate people.
Team building builds trust and compatible ways of working; pay and career progression may be outside the PM's remit.

summary: You can now explain what makes a PRINCE2 team effective: a diverse, well-matched mix of capabilities, competencies and perspectives, with roles fitted to each person's capability, authority and availability. You can also describe how to find and close gaps by upskilling or shifting tasks.

A.q: What does PRINCE2 say an effective project team requires?
options: Members with matching skills so that roles are interchangeable
A team drawn from one department to simplify reporting lines
Standard role descriptions applied the same way on every project
A diverse mix of capabilities, competencies and perspectives
A.why: An effective team needs a diverse set of capabilities, competencies and perspectives that match the project's requirements (manual 3.3.2).

whyNot.0: PRINCE2 values diversity; it also notes people with the same skills perform roles differently.
whyNot.1: Projects typically work across organizational boundaries; one department rarely supplies the mix needed.
whyNot.2: Generic standard role descriptions are unlikely to be effective; roles should fit the individual.

A.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. Roles and responsibilities should reflect the capability, authority and [?] of the individual doing the work.
options: seniority
availability
qualifications
location
A.why: Roles should reflect capability, authority and availability, considered through key relationships (manual 3.3.2).

whyNot.0: Seniority is not one of the three factors; team members may even be more senior than the project manager.
whyNot.2: Qualifications are not one of the three factors; PRINCE2 focuses on capability.
whyNot.3: Location affects how teams communicate, but it is not one of the three factors named for roles.

A.q: A project manager finds that an analyst assigned to data migration testing has no experience of it. What does PRINCE2 recommend?
options: Escalate the gap to the business layer as a project exception
Accept the gap, as the analyst holds a recognized qualification
Mitigate it, for example by upskilling or shifting those tasks
Record the gap in the risk management approach for the board
A.why: PRINCE2 expects gaps in competencies and capabilities to be identified and mitigated, for example by upskilling or shifting responsibilities for certain tasks to more appropriate people (manual 3.3.2).

whyNot.0: A project exception is a forecast breach of project tolerance; a skills gap is handled within the project.
whyNot.1: A qualification does not guarantee competence in a specific task; the gap still needs mitigating.
whyNot.3: The risk management approach holds procedures, not specific situations; the gap needs a mitigation.

B.q:
Which two statements about effective teams are correct?
1. People with the same capabilities may perform the same role differently.
2. Generic standard role descriptions are usually the most effective option.
3. The same person may perform differently depending on who they work with.
4. Pay and career progression are within the project manager's control.
options: 1 and 3
1 and 2
2 and 4
3 and 4
B.why: PRINCE2 notes that people with the same capabilities perform roles differently (1) and that one person may perform differently with different colleagues (3) (manual 3.3.2).

whyNot.1: Statement 2 is false: generic standard role descriptions are unlikely to be effective.
whyNot.2: Both are false: standard role descriptions are unlikely to work, and pay and career progression may be outside the PM's remit.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is false: some motivators, such as pay and career progression, may be outside the PM's remit.

B.q: Why are generic, standard role descriptions unlikely to be effective on a PRINCE2 project?
options: PRINCE2 does not use role descriptions for project board roles
Role descriptions are written by the business layer after closure
Roles should reflect each person's capability, authority and availability
Each PRINCE2 role has to be filled by a different person on every project
B.why: Roles should reflect the capability, authority and availability of the individual and be considered through their key relationships (manual 3.3.2).

whyNot.0: Role descriptions cover all project management team roles, including the board.
whyNot.1: Role descriptions are prepared when the project management team is designed, not after closure.
whyNot.3: PRINCE2 allows one person to hold several roles within the rules, so this is not the reason.

B.q: Halfway through a project, a key supplier contact is replaced and the working relationship with a team manager changes. What does PRINCE2 suggest about the roles affected?
options: Leave them unchanged until the project is closed
Review and update them in light of the new relationship
Ask the business layer to reissue the project mandate
Merge the team manager role into the project board
B.why: Roles and responsibilities should be reviewed when key relationships shift, and updated accordingly (manual 3.3.2).

whyNot.0: Waiting until closure ignores PRINCE2's guidance to review roles when key relationships shift.
whyNot.2: The project mandate triggers the project; a change in a working relationship does not require a new one.
whyNot.3: Team managers work at the delivering level; merging the role into the board would break the levels of organization.

C.q: A project manager wants a newly formed, mixed team to work well together quickly. Which action does PRINCE2 suggest, and why?
options: Issue work packages at once, because tolerances build trust
Offer pay rises, because motivation is the PM's responsibility
Hold a lessons review, because learning precedes delivery
Use structured team building, which speeds up team formation
C.why: Structured team-building exercises can accelerate team building, helping build trust and compatible ways of working (manual 3.3.2).

whyNot.0: Tolerances support management by exception; they are not how PRINCE2 says trust is built in a new team.
whyNot.1: Pay may be outside the project manager's remit, so it is not the suggested route.
whyNot.2: Seeking lessons is valuable, but it is not the action PRINCE2 names for accelerating team formation.

C.q: A project manager knows a team member is motivated mainly by promotion prospects. Which statement reflects PRINCE2 guidance?
options: Promotion may lie outside the PM's remit, which shapes how they lead
The PM should promise promotion to secure the member's commitment
Motivation is a matter for the project board, not the PM
The member should be swapped for someone motivated by the work
C.why: PRINCE2 notes that some motivational factors, such as remuneration and career progression, may be outside the project manager's remit; this affects how they lead the team (manual 3.3).

whyNot.1: Promising something outside the PM's remit is not supported by PRINCE2 guidance.
whyNot.2: Motivating people is part of leadership, which the project manager carries out too.
whyNot.3: Roles should reflect capability, authority and availability, not a particular motivation.

C.q: A project needs engineering, finance and community-relations skills. The project manager notes that two engineers with identical qualifications perform quite differently. Which conclusion is correct?
options: Qualifications should decide roles, as the capability is equal
The team should be narrowed to engineers to reduce variation
Roles should be matched to people, not assumed from paperwork
Both engineers should share one role so output averages out
C.why: The project needs a diverse mix matched to its needs, and people with the same capabilities perform roles differently, so roles should reflect each person (manual 3.3.2).

whyNot.0: Equal qualifications do not mean equal performance in a role; PRINCE2 expects roles to fit the individual.
whyNot.1: The project needs diverse capabilities and perspectives; narrowing the mix works against that.
whyNot.3: Sharing a role does not address fit; roles should reflect each person's capability, authority and availability.

reteach.title: Forming a band
reteach.question: Would four excellent guitarists make a good band?

blocks.h: The right mix, fitted to the people
blocks.body: A band needs a drummer, a bassist, a singer and a guitarist: a diverse mix matched to the music. Two drummers with the same training still play differently, and a drummer may play better beside one bassist than another. If the singer cannot reach the high notes, you coach them or give that line to someone else. That is effective team building in PRINCE2 terms.

blocks.text: A music certificate does not guarantee someone can play this set tonight. Check competence for the actual work.

explain.body: An effective team has a diverse set of capabilities, competencies and perspectives, chosen to match what this project requires.

test.q: Which best describes the make-up of an effective PRINCE2 project team?
options: Uniform skills so that people are interchangeable
Diverse capabilities matched to the project's needs
Members drawn from the supplier organization
The most senior staff available in the business
test.why: PRINCE2 calls for a diverse set of capabilities, competencies and perspectives matched to the project (manual 3.3.2).

whyNot.0: Uniform skills reduce diversity, and people with the same skills still perform differently.
whyNot.2: Projects combine business, user and supplier people; one source rarely provides the mix.
whyNot.3: Seniority is not the test; capability, authority and availability are.

explain.body: Roles should reflect the capability, authority and availability of the individual, be considered through their key relationships and be reviewed when those relationships shift.

test.q: Which three factors should roles and responsibilities reflect?
options: Grade, salary and location
Qualification, seniority and tenure
Experience, cost and department
Capability, authority and availability
test.why: Manual 3.3.2 names capability, authority and availability.

whyNot.0: Grade, salary and location are not the factors PRINCE2 names.
whyNot.1: Qualifications and seniority do not guarantee fit for a role.
whyNot.2: These are not the three factors PRINCE2 names for roles.

explain.body: Understand the competencies and capabilities of those assigned, identify gaps, and put mitigations in place, for example upskilling or shifting responsibility for certain tasks to more appropriate people.

test.q: Which are examples of mitigating a competency gap in PRINCE2?
options: Upskilling or shifting tasks to more suitable people
Raising an exception report or a request for change
Lowering the quality criteria for affected products
Extending the stage to give people more time
test.why: Manual 3.3.2 gives upskilling and shifting responsibilities for certain tasks as examples.

whyNot.1: Exception reports and requests for change deal with tolerances and baselines, not skills gaps.
whyNot.2: Quality criteria come from what users need; lowering them does not close a skills gap.
whyNot.3: Stage length is a planning decision and does not build the missing competence.

explain.body: Structured team-building exercises can accelerate how a team forms, building trust and finding compatible ways of working.

test.q: What is team building intended to achieve, according to PRINCE2?
options: Approval of the stage plan by the board
A shorter list of project stakeholders
Trust and compatible ways of working
Agreement of project-level tolerances
test.why: Team building aims to build trust and find compatible ways of working (Quick Reference Guide, manual 3.3.2).

whyNot.0: Stage plans are approved by the board in 'directing a project'.
whyNot.1: Stakeholders are identified through stakeholder analysis, not reduced by team building.
whyNot.3: Project tolerances are set by the business layer.
